title: kv-cache-threshold-oscillation-batching-latency-synthesis
content:
Summary:

This note collects the incident review and runbook draft for the Nov 1-2 2025 flapping incident where free memory on a subset of serving nodes oscillated, triggering repeated large continuous-batching flushes and transient OOMs in the runtime. Impact was intermittent 95th/99th token latency spikes for customer traffic and two short-lived process restarts before autoscaling recovered capacity.

Observed symptoms (high level):
- Beginning ~2025-11-01T22:10 UTC: subset of nodes showed memory usage climb from 45% -> 92% over ~15m on models with long prefix workloads.
- Automatic batcher started emitting larger-than-expected batches (avg batch size increased 3x for affected routes) causing per-request p99 token latency spikes.
- Two runtime processes reached RSS > node alloc and were OOM-killed by kernel. Kube restarted them; readiness probes delayed by cache warmup, contributing to error rate bump.
- Eviction/compaction subsystem logs show repeated small-window cache evictions and re-population churn (cache-index flip events).

Root-cause hypothesis (working):
- A recent change to the KV-cache admission threshold (PR 1289) created a feedback loop under certain request-mix patterns: when cache hit-rate drops below ~12% for a prefix, the admission controller lowered the per-key retention threshold to reclaim space. That shrink caused more misses for slightly different prefixes, causing rapid repopulation and extra memory allocations during continuous-batching prefetch paths.
- Combined with a nightly workload skew (longer prefixes + high concurrency from an internal CI job) the oscillation amplitude exceeded the cache compaction cadence and pushed memory beyond our soft-limits.
- Continuous batcher had a subtle timing interaction: large batches allocate larger attention KV state and hold it briefly during kernel calls, amplifying the memory spike.

Timeline (extracted from logs + metrics):
- 2025-11-01T22:08 UTC: spike in in-flight requests for route /chat/long-prefix (CI-simulated traffic ramp).
- 2025-11-01T22:10 UTC: cache-admission metrics show drop in effective eviction threshold (metric: cache.admission.retention_bytes) from 1.2GB -> 400MB over 40s.
- 2025-11-01T22:12 UTC: batcher.average_size climbs from 6 -> 18 for affected model instance.
- 2025-11-01T22:20 UTC: node-3 process OOM (killed by kernel), pod restarted.
- 2025-11-01T22:25 UTC: autoscaler brought up an extra replica; p90 latencies largely recovered but p99 remained noisy for ~20m.
- 2025-11-01T22:37 UTC: second OOM on node-7 during recovery period.
- 2025-11-01T23:05 UTC: ops team applied emergency admission floor to 600MB and temporarily disabled aggressive prefetch for the route; memory stabilized.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident:
- Emergency admission floor set to 600MB for all KV caches (ops-only feature flag).
- Continuous-batcher max batch size reduced from 32 -> 12 for three noisy models to limit transient allocation spikes.
- Temporary scheduled cleanup hook run to compact fragmented caches on recovered pods.

Post-incident action items (short term):
1) Revert or patch PR 1289 behavior: add hysteresis to admission threshold changes (owner: Marcus Chen, ETA: 2025-11-12).
2) Add guardrails in batcher: an allocation-budget check that refuses batches if projected KV allocation would exceed per-pod soft-limit (owner: Lina Park, ETA: 2025-11-19).
3) Improve rollout checklist: any cache/admission tuning must include stress-tests with mixed prefix-length workloads and CI simulated load (owner: eng-release, ETA: 2025-11-17).
4) Instrument per-prefix churn metric (cache.prefix.churn_rate) and an alert when churn_rate > 0.2 for >3m (owner: Diego Alvarez, ETA: 2025-11-10).

Runbook draft / Triage checklist (for on-call):
- Page SRE on-call with subject: "KV cache oscillation suspected". Include basic metrics links and whether autoscaler created replicas.
- Identify impacted model routes: query metrics: 
  - PromQL: sum by(route) (increase(cache.evictions_total[5m])) > 50 -> candidate routes
  - PromQL: topk(10, cache.admission.retention_bytes) to find low-retention caches
- If memory climb observed: set temporary cache admission floor: 
  - /ops/flags set kv_cache_admission_min_bytes=600000000 (ops-only endpoint).
- Reduce continuous-batcher max size for impacted model instances: 
  - admin API: PATCH /admin/models/{id}/config {"batcher.max_items": 12}
- If OOM occurred and pod restarted: check readiness delay and trigger manual cache compact on restart: 
  - kubectl exec -c runtime $POD -- /usr/local/bin/kvcache-compact --max-latency-ms=200
- If repeated restarts across nodes: scale up reserved capacity and notify platform-eng for emergency node eviction window.

Diagnostic queries and commands (quick reference):
- PromQL:  increase(node_memory_RSS_bytes[5m]) by (pod) to see RSS ramps
- PromQL:  rate(batch_allocations_bytes[1m]) > 0 to find allocation bursts aligned with batcher events
- Logs: grep for "admission threshold" and "prefetch" in runtime logs: 
  - rg "admission|prefetch|churn|evict" /var/log/runtime/*.log --context 3
- Heap proto dump (if node alive, attach gcore): 
  - kubectl debug --copy-to=debug-$POD --image=ubuntu -- attach gcore -p $(pidof runtime)
- Flamegraph of allocation hotspots (postmortem): run eBPF off-sample and aggregate over 60s window during spike.

Monitoring / alerting updates proposed:
- New alert: Cache prefix churn high: cache.prefix.churn_rate > 0.2 for 3m -> P2.
- New alert: Batch allocation burst: increase(batch_allocations_bytes[1m]) > 200MB -> P2.
- Adjust existing OOM run alert to include recent readiness-delay check so SRE knows to watch for readiness probe failures post-restart.

Open questions and unknowns:
- Why did the admission controller pick such an aggressive retention reduction for a single prefix class? Need to inspect policy matrix and weight function used in PR 1289.
- Are there long-tail prefixes that unavoidable cause repopulation on each request due to tokenization differences? If so, consider prefix-normalization or canonicalization at admission time.
- Does the allocator fragmentation pattern contribute more than raw bytes? The compact hook reduced RSS by ~80MB in runs we sampled, but not enough to explain full spike. Need deeper heap-profiling.

Follow-ups (owners assigned):
- Marcus Chen: create PR to add hysteresis + rate-limit to admission changes; include unit tests and canary in staging (ETA 2025-11-12).
- Lina Park: implement batcher allocation budget check & limiter, add e2e with mixed-length prompt simulation (ETA 2025-11-19).
- Diego Alvarez: add cache.prefix.churn_rate metric, dashboard & alert (ETA 2025-11-10).
- Eng-release: update rollout checklist and require perf regression approval for cache/admission configs (ETA 2025-11-17).

Notes to reviewers / contextual links:
- The working hypothesis ties two subsystems (admission + batcher) and a workload skew. If reviewers see other plausible root causes (allocator fragmentation, prefetch race), add comments and attach profiling artifacts.
- Attachments: staged heap dumps, flamegraphs, timeline chart (links in linked_artifacts).

Internal blips and low-priority observations we noticed but did not act on during incident:
- Slight increase in gc cycles for Python shim on some hosts, likely noise.
- One older model variant had an out-of-date quantization kernel; perf team will audit model builds.

Draft runbook excerpt to be copied into canonical runbooks/serving-runtime-ooms.md when validated:
- Trigger conditions: rising pod RSS > 75% of soft-limit AND batcher.average_size > 2x baseline for 5m -> run triage playbook A.
- Playbook A: set admission floor -> throttle prefetch -> reduce batcher.max_items -> monitor for 10m -> scale out if not recovered.

Decision log (short):
- Emergency floor chosen because it provides fastest mitigation with minimal behavioral change to code paths.
- Longer-term fix must avoid oscillation by design (hysteresis + bounded-rate changes).

Status: in_review. Please add comments inline (GH: linked_artifacts PR/issue) and flag if this should be elevated to a full postmortem write-up.

-- end of note --
